items.title: ‘Let Your Child Enjoy the Rain’: Paediatrician Busts 4 Common Fears About Kids Falling Sick
items.blurb: The first drops of rain can bring out two very different reactions at home. While children may be eager to run outside, jump in puddles and feel the rain on their faces, parents are often quick to say, ‘You’ll catch a cold,’ or ‘You’ll get a fever.’ But does getting wet really make children sick? Can playing in the rain weaken their immunity? And should parents rush them indoors the moment it starts raining? There are plenty of beliefs around children and rain, and science draws a clearer line between genuine risks and common myths. In a conversation with The Better India , Dr Shravan Krishna Reddy , a paediatrician, neonatologist and paediatric nutritionist who co-founded The Family Tree Hospital in Tirupati, breaks down some of the most common monsoon myths. Here’s what he wants parents to know before they say “no” to every rainy-day adventure. Myth 1: Playing in the rain causes a cold Fact: Rain itself does not cause a cold. “A common cold is caused by respiratory viruses — not by raindrops, wet clothes or cold water,” explains Dr Reddy. So why do the two seem so closely connected? During the rainy season, children may spend more time in crowded school vehicles or poorly ventilated classrooms, where viruses can spread more easily. A child may also already be incubating a virus when they play in the rain. If symptoms appear the following day, it is easy to blame the most recent event. “ Doctor, yesterday he played in the rain. Today he has a fever .” A few minutes of rain play can be a childhood memory worth keeping. The key is knowing when the weather and surroundings are safe. Photograph: ( Shutterstock ) Dr Reddy says he hears this sentence almost every week during the monsoon. “The timing may be related, but rain is not the infection. Somewhere along the way, the child has picked up a virus — or another illness altogether.” In other words, getting wet is not the same as getting infected. Myth 2: Children should never play in the rain Fact: Healthy children can enjoy occasional rain play — if the conditions are safe. “A healthy child can occasionally play in light, clean rain under adult supervision,” says Dr Reddy. Rain gives children a chance to move, play outdoors and experience nature firsthand, from the sound of raindrops to the feel of water under their feet. It can also become a happy childhood memory. The surroundings, however, matter. Stagnant roadside puddles, open drains, construction sites, slippery terraces, flooded areas and thunderstorms are best avoided. Children should also wear footwear with a good grip. “The benefit does not come from rain magically ‘boosting immunity’. It comes from movement, outdoor play, confidence, sensory experience and happiness,” Dr Reddy explains. His advice is simple: “Let your child enjoy 10 sensible minutes of clean rain rather than spend childhood being frightened of weather.” Myth 3: Getting wet weakens immunity Fact: One rainy-day shower does not damage a child’s immune system. “Immunity is not a battery that loses charge because a child got drenched,” says Dr Reddy. When a fever follows a rainy-day adventure, the rain isn’t necessarily to blame. Parents should watch for symptoms and focus on how the child is doing. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) A child may feel cold , uncomfortable, or tired after wearing wet clothes for too long. Children with asthma may also experience symptoms triggered by cold air, humidity, mould, or an existing respiratory infection. But that is different from saying rain has weakened their immunity. According to Dr Reddy, parents should focus on the things that genuinely support immune health: adequate sleep, balanced nutrition, timely vaccinations, physical activity, clean air and avoiding tobacco smoke. Myth 4: Fever after rain means the child needs antibiotics Fact: Rain does not cause fever, and fever does not automatically mean antibiotics are needed. “Getting wet does not directly generate a fever — fever is the body's response to infection or inflammation, and rain is neither,” says Dr Reddy. A child who develops fever after playing in the rain could have a respiratory viral infection or another illness, depending on the symptoms and local disease patterns. The real monsoon risks are often around the rain: stagnant water, open drains, slippery surfaces, mosquitoes and electrical hazards — not the raindrops themselves. Photograph: ( Bhaskar English ) He has seen parents arrive at the hospital having already started several medicines at home simply because their child played in the rain and then developed a fever. “That is where unnecessary treatment begins: an antibiotic for a viral illness, a syrup for a cough that would have settled on its own, and a family convinced the rain was to blame.” His advice? Watch the child, not just the thermometer. Notice how they are behaving between fever episodes. Are they drinking enough fluids, passing urine normally, responding to you and breathing comfortably? Seek medical attention if the child is breathing fast or struggling to breathe, vomiting repeatedly, unusually drowsy or confused, passing much less urine, or develops abdominal pain, a rash, seizures or a fever that lasts beyond three days. “Rain is not a diagnosis. A fever after rain deserves the same careful assessment as a fever in any other week.” So, when should parents actually say no? Dr Reddy says the conditions matter more than the calendar. A gentle drizzle, clean surroundings, good visibility and a healthy child are very different from heavy rain accompanied by flooding, strong winds, thunder, lightning, open electrical wiring or overflowing drains. “Parents do not have to choose between being careless and being excessively fearful. There is a sensible middle path.” That middle path looks different depending on the child. A school-going child who is healthy and eager to splash around may be fine with a few supervised minutes in the rain. With a newborn, young infant or premature baby, parents need to be more cautious. The same applies when a child is already unwell, wheezing, or has certain chronic or immune-compromising conditions, Dr Reddy says. Getting wet doesn’t cause a cold. Respiratory viruses do — which is why understanding the real risks can help parents worry less. Photograph: (Dr Shravan Reddy) And during a thunderstorm, the rule is simple: go indoors. “When thunder is heard, children move indoors immediately – and outdoor activity does not resume until at least 30 minutes after the last thunder.” What parents should really watch out for According to Dr Reddy, many of the genuine risks of monsoon play come from the environment around the rain. Floodwater and stagnant water can contain sewage, animal waste, chemicals and sharp objects. Mosquito breeding can increase the risk of diseases such as dengue and malaria, while contaminated water can contribute to diarrhoeal illnesses and infections. Slippery surfaces, open drains, fallen branches, electrical hazards and fast-moving water can also pose immediate risks. “Rain itself is not the villain. Contaminated water, unsafe surroundings and delayed recognition of illness are the real concerns.” Ultimately, Dr Reddy believes children should be protected without being made afraid of ordinary childhood experiences. “From years of treating children and speaking with thousands of parents, I have learned that childhood needs both protection and freedom.” A little rain can be part of childhood, with parents teaching children when it is safe to splash outside and when it is time to head indoors.

items.title: How 2000 Chennai Residents Turned a Sewage-Choked 50-Acre Lake Into a Lively Public Space
items.blurb: Picture a fifty-acre lake right behind your house. Now picture still having to buy water in cans to drink, cook and bathe, because the lake outside your window is too choked with sewage and garbage to give you a single drop. That was daily life in Chitlapakkam, a residential neighbourhood near Chennai, for years. Today, the same lake recharges the groundwater beneath the town , and residents walk laps around it every evening instead of queuing for water tankers. Getting from one reality to the other took seven years, a volunteer group called Chitlapakkam Rising, and a stubborn refusal to let a "dying lake" stay that way. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) A water crisis with a lake next door The crisis wasn't abstract for long. By 2016, borewells across Chitlapakkam had started running dry , and the ones that hadn't were pulling up water that looked closer to sludge. "There wasn't even a drop of water in our homes. Some people even noticed contaminated black water in their borewell. Despite several protests, there was no action by the government. I had to pay for water, with a lake right in my backyard," recalls Dayanand Krishnan, a civil engineer who would go on to advise Chitlapakkam Rising. The lake itself, believed to be around a hundred years old, told the story of that neglect. One side had become a dumping ground; the other was choked with water hyacinth. Locals had stopped calling it by its real name and started calling it Saakadai Eri instead — the Sewage Lake. Years of civic action led to one bigger fight Chitlapakkam wasn't starting from scratch. Its citizens' welfare associations date back to the late 1980s, and had already proven they could win fights that mattered, once forming a human chain to stop a state housing board from building over parts of the lake. More than 2,000 residents came together to clean Chitlapakkam Lake in 2019. Photograph: (AI-Generated collage) But it took the devastating Chennai floods of December 2015 , and the grim realisation that a neglected lake had made the flooding worse, to turn decades of civic muscle into a single, focused campaign. In 2017, the tactics were still patient ones: postcards, petitions, street plays, songs, anything that might make the government look up. Two years of that got them almost nowhere. 2,000 people, one lake, and a turning point So in 2019, residents stopped waiting for permission and picked up gloves themselves. "The lake was inaccessible due to years of neglect. Despite years of efforts in the form of postcards, petitions, protests, candlelight vigils, the government didn't pay heed. That's when we planned the mass cleaning drive," says Sunil Jayaram, one of the founding members of Chitlapakkam Rising. On 2 June 2019, over 2,000 people showed up. Not for one weekend, but for several, under the banner #SavingChitlapakkamLake, until word spread far enough on social media that the state could no longer look away. The following year, the then Chief Minister visited in person and sanctioned ₹25 crore in the assembly for the lake's restoration. Chitlapakkam Rising’s seven-year campaign transformed a polluted waterbody into a community space. "Social activism runs in the DNA of the people of Chitlapakkam," says L Sundararaman, president of the Chitlapakkam Muthulakshmi Nagar Welfare Association, who has watched the neighbourhood fight for this lake since he moved here in 1987. The 4D plan that revived the lake Money alone doesn't fix a hundred-year-old lake. Restoring it scientifically needed a method, and Chitlapakkam Rising had one ready: a four-step process the team calls the 4D model. First, sluice gates were built at every inlet, deflecting incoming sewage to a treatment plant instead of the lake. Next, the sewage water already trapped inside for years was drained out through a sluice outlet, leaving the lake bed dry. The contaminated soil was then desilted entirely, before the lake was deepened by 2.5 metres, based on soil studies, to hold more rainwater and keep the neighbourhood from flooding again. The restored lake now features walking paths, greenery, an open-air gym and spaces for recreation. Step by step, a sewage-choked waterbody became a functioning lake again, not just a cleaner-looking one. From ‘sewage lake’ to evening walks Restoring the water was never really the finish line. What Chitlapakkam wanted was its water security back, and a neighbourhood worth living in. So residents were asked, through a Facebook poll, what they wanted built around the revived lake. Today, the answer stands there in full: a walking path, an open-air gym, an amphitheatre, a basketball court, stretches of greenery, all wrapped around water that once forced people to buy their own supply. Mornings and evenings now find the same lakeside crowded with walkers, children, and senior citizens, not garbage. Since October 2023, Chitlapakkam Rising has started conducting lake walk tours for residents of other localities hoping to pull off the same transformation where they live. What began as a fight to save a dying lake became a community-led movement for water security and better public spaces. A fifty-acre lake sitting dead behind your house is easy to walk past every single day. It took seven years, but the people of Chitlapakkam never did. About the campaign This story is part of The Better India's #CivicSenseHeroes , a year-long nationwide campaign celebrating citizens who take responsibility for the places and communities we all share. From cleaner streets and safer roads to restored lakes and public spaces, we're looking for everyday Indians turning civic sense into action. Know someone doing work like this? items.title: Inside India’s Food-Safety Crackdown: How Officers Make Kitchens, Dairies & Warehouses Accountable
items.blurb: A restaurant kitchen can look immaculate from the dining room. A milk tanker can look like any other on the highway. A packet of paneer can carry a familiar brand name. The problem begins where the consumer cannot see. Inside warehouses, kitchens, dairies and processing units, food-safety officers are looking for what a label cannot reveal: expired products, poor refrigeration, unsafe handling, adulteration and conditions in which food can become a public-health risk. Across India, 2025 and 2026 have seen food-safety enforcement move beyond the familiar pre-Diwali raid. Surprise inspections, laboratory testing, licence suspensions, seizures and destruction of unsafe food are becoming part of wider state-level campaigns. At the centre of one of the most visible crackdowns is Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra’s Food and Drug Administration commissioner. But his campaign is one part of a wider shift, with officers such as Roshan Jacob in Uttar Pradesh , T Shubhamangala in Rajasthan and Kanwalpreet Brar in Punjab approaching food safety through enforcement, surveillance, testing and education. Maharashtra: Tukaram Mundhe takes the fight inside the kitchen When Tukaram Mundhe took charge of Maharashtra’s FDA in May 2026, inspections became a public affair. Between 25 May and 31 July, the department inspected 3,137 hotels, restaurants, eateries and other establishments. It suspended 165 licences and seized or destroyed 28.66 lakh kg of unsafe food valued at Rs 55.72 crore. Mundhe has led the suspension of food permits of four Domino's and one Pizza Hut outlet in recent weeks, and has also targeted cricket clubs, hotels and well-known restaurants in over 3,000 raids. Photograph: (X/Tukaram_IndIAS) The inspections did not stop at small eateries. FDA teams visited restaurants, dairies, hotel kitchens, warehouses, canteens and food businesses connected to delivery platforms. In August, the department inspected 86 establishments involved in online food sales and delivery, issuing 60 improvement notices and suspending 14 licences linked to platforms including Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. Just Speak FDA Maharashtra has launched grievance redressal portal for citizens. It is AI enabled platform, having auto assignment, auto escalation and built in accountability with traceability features . https://t.co/597si71Z6E #TukaramMundhe #FDA — Tukaram Mundhe (@Tukaram_IndIAS) July 15, 2026 The violations have ranged from poor storage and refrigeration to sanitation failures and expired products. Five restaurants at Mumbai Cricket Association premises , for instance, had their licences suspended after inspections found problems involving food storage, handling, refrigeration and sanitation. On 20 August, Mundhe issued another warning, this time to consumers, advising them against buying loose or unsealed edible oil because of the risks of adulteration, unsafe packaging and the absence of proper quality controls. The argument, then, is no longer simply about conducting more raids. It is about how aggressively a regulator should act when it believes public health is at risk. Uttar Pradesh: Roshan Jacob takes adulteration to scale In Uttar Pradesh, Roshan Jacob was appointed Secretary and Commissioner of the Food Safety and Drug Administration Department in September 2025. Her first major test came with the Diwali season. From 8 to 17 October 2025, the state ran a special enforcement campaign involving 6,075 inspections and 2,740 raids. Teams collected 3,767 samples and seized 3,548 quintals of adulterated or suspicious material worth about Rs 4.97 crore. Another 1,871 quintals of harmful material, valued at Rs 2.89 crore, was destroyed. The seizures showed how adulteration travels through everyday food. In different districts, officials intercepted paneer, khoya, sweets, milk products, oils and ghee. At one point, 4,040 kg of khoya was seized on NH-34, while 910 cartons of adulterated sweets were intercepted at a Barabanki toll point. The important part was what came next: the state said market surveillance would continue beyond the festival, rather than allowing enforcement to disappear with the Diwali calendar. Rajasthan: The answer is not only punishment Rajasthan’s Food Safety Commissioner T Shubhamangala has taken a different route alongside enforcement: train the people who handle food before violations happen. On 17 March 2026, more than 30,000 food-business operators and related workers were trained on the first day of a two-day programme under the state’s “Shuddh Aahar–Milavat Par Vaar” campaign. The target was 50,000 people. The trainees were not limited to restaurant owners. They included anganwadi workers, mid-day meal staff, government hostel employees, jail kitchen workers, hotel and dhaba operators and street-food vendors. Rajasthan has also been working towards digital inspections and wider access to food testing, including mobile laboratories, bringing testing closer to producers and sellers rather than relying only on central laboratories. Photograph: (economictimes) It changes the question from How many adulterators can we catch? to another one: How many unsafe practices can we prevent? Rajasthan has also been working towards digital inspections and wider access to food testing, including mobile laboratories, bringing testing closer to producers and sellers rather than relying only on central laboratories. Punjab: Following milk from farm to market Punjab’s Kanwalpreet Brar has focused on one of the state’s most important food chains: dairy. On 7 and 8 May 2026, Punjab carried out a statewide milk-sampling drive. Teams collected 204 samples from dairy farms, milk collection centres, processing units and retail outlets across urban and rural areas. The results showed why sampling matters. Of the 204 samples tested, 68 failed quality checks and one was found unsafe for drinking. The department subsequently launched a statewide paneer-sampling drive, collecting 211 samples from dairies, processing units and retailers. Kanwalpreet Brar, Punjab executed an intensive statewide milk-sampling drive on May 6 and 7, 2026, collecting 204 samples to crack down on milk adulteration. Photograph: (punjab itribune online) Brar has also stressed education, asking food-safety officers to help businesses understand hygienic handling and storage rather than relying only on penalties. The bigger fight is the invisible one The four approaches are different. Mundhe has made inspections highly visible. Jacob has demonstrated what statewide surveillance can uncover. Shubhamangala is pairing enforcement with training and technology. Brar is following a food chain, milk and dairy through repeated sampling. Food safety begins long before a meal reaches the table. It involves the tanker carrying milk, the warehouse storing beverages, the kitchen refrigerator, the paneer-processing unit, the street-food cart and increasingly, the warehouse from which a ten-minute delivery is dispatched. That is why the most important number may not be the number of raids. It is whether the next consumer eventually stops having to wonder what is really on the plate. items.title: The Fascinating Science of How India’s Fish Survive in Freshwater and the Sea
items.blurb: A rui (rohu) can spend its life in a pond in Bengal without drinking much water. A bangda (Indian mackerel) in the Arabian Sea faces the opposite challenge: surrounded by saltwater, it must prevent too much water from leaving its body. Put them on ice at a fish market and the difference may seem purely culinary. One might end up in a Bengali jhol ; the other could become a crisp fry or a coconut-based curry. But beneath their scales is a biological divide that has shaped how they breathe, drink, eat and survive. The difference begins with the chemistry of the water around them. India’s fish live across an extraordinary range of habitats — Himalayan rivers, floodplain wetlands, village ponds, reservoirs, mangroves, estuaries, coastal lagoons and nearly 7,500 km of coastline. For fish living in these environments, survival depends on constantly maintaining the right balance of water and salt inside their bodies. The body versus the water The central principle is osmosis — the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane in response to differences in the concentration of dissolved substances. A freshwater fish such as rohu, catla, mrigal, mahseer or magur has body fluids that are saltier than the water around it. As a result, water naturally tends to enter its body. That creates a problem. Cells need a stable concentration of salts and other dissolved substances to function. If too much water enters, that balance can be disturbed. Marine species such as surmai, bangda and pomfret often have firmer flesh, while oily fish such as mackerel and sardines contain more fat. Photograph: (Jason Holland) Freshwater fish have evolved an efficient way to deal with this. They generally drink very little water. Instead, they produce large quantities of dilute urine to remove excess water, while specialised cells in their gills actively take up essential salts from the surrounding water. Marine bony fish face the reverse situation. Seawater is generally saltier than the body fluids of species such as Indian mackerel, sardines and many pomfrets. Water therefore tends to move out of their bodies. To compensate, many marine fish drink seawater, absorb the water they need and use their gills and kidneys to remove excess salts. In simple terms, a freshwater fish is trying to prevent itself from becoming too diluted. A marine fish is trying not to lose too much water. This continuous balancing act is called osmoregulation. Fish that live between two worlds The divide becomes more complicated where rivers meet the sea. India’s estuaries, mangroves, backwaters and coastal lagoons contain brackish water, where freshwater and seawater mix. Salinity can rise and fall with tides, rainfall and river flow. Chilika Lagoon in Odisha, Pulicat Lake along the Andhra Pradesh-Tamil Nadu coast, Kerala’s backwaters and the Sundarbans are among these transition zones. Fish living in such habitats must cope with water whose chemistry can change over time. Some species can adjust their salt-and-water regulation as they move between different salinities. The hilsa, or ilish, is one of India’s best-known examples. An anadromous fish, it spends much of its life in marine or coastal waters before migrating into freshwater rivers to breed. During this journey, its body must adapt to changing salinity. These ecosystems are also important for fisheries and aquaculture, supporting species such as pearlspot, Asian seabass and milkfish. Their health matters not only for biodiversity but also for communities whose food and livelihoods depend on the shifting boundary between river and sea. From rui to bangda The science changes from one habitat to another, but India’s relationship with fish is also reflected in language. In Bengal and across parts of the Ganga-Brahmaputra basin, rohu is widely known as rui, while catla is commonly called katla. Mrigal, bata, pabda, magur and koi are also familiar names in eastern markets, although local names can vary across regions and languages. In the sea, small pelagic fish such as sardines and mackerel feed heavily on plankton, while larger predators may eat smaller fish, squid and crustaceans. Photograph: (PTI) On the west coast, Indian mackerel is known as bangda in Maharashtra. Pomfret is commonly called paplet in parts of the Konkan and Gujarat, while sardines are known as mathi or chaala in parts of Kerala. Freshwater aquaculture has also made species such as rohu and catla widely available in inland markets. In recent years, efforts to replenish indigenous fish populations in rivers have sought to connect conservation with the livelihoods of fishing communities. Marine fisheries, meanwhile, remain closely tied to the rhythms of the sea. Seasonal fishing restrictions during the monsoon — imposed for different periods depending on the coast and fishing zone — can affect the availability of wild-caught marine fish while allowing time for breeding and stock replenishment. What reaches the plate The biological differences between freshwater and marine fish do not automatically determine how a fish should be cooked. Fat content, texture, bone structure, size and freshness often matter more. Still, these differences can often be noticed on the plate. Freshwater species such as rohu, catla and tilapia are generally mild in flavour. Their flesh works well in curries, stews and other preparations where moisture helps keep the fish from drying out. Marine species such as surmai, bangda and pomfret often have firmer flesh, while oily fish such as mackerel and sardines contain more fat. These qualities make many of them well suited to frying, grilling, roasting and coastal curries. Their nutritional profiles can also differ by species. Fish are generally good sources of protein and vitamin B12. Oily fish such as mackerel and sardines are particularly known for their omega-3 fatty acids. Some marine fish can also contribute nutrients such as iodine and selenium. The exact nutritional value, however, depends on the species, portion and method of preparation. Price and availability follow a similar pattern. Farmed freshwater fish are often more consistently available in inland markets, while the price of marine fish can vary with season, catch, species and distance from the coast. A rohu may be an everyday purchase in one city; surmai may be a premium fish in another. A food web beneath the water What fish eat also depends on their species and ecological role. Rohu feeds largely on phytoplankton, algae and plant matter, while other freshwater fish may feed on insects, plankton, crustaceans or smaller fish. In the sea, small pelagic fish such as sardines and mackerel feed heavily on plankton, while larger predators may eat smaller fish, squid and crustaceans. Together, they form links in a much larger food web. Small fish transfer energy from microscopic organisms to larger animals. Predatory fish help regulate prey populations. Fish also move nutrients through ecosystems and connect habitats that may appear separate on a map. That is why the story of a fish does not end at the market. Freshwater species depend on functioning rivers, wetlands, floodplains and ponds. Marine species need healthy coastal and ocean ecosystems. Fish that move through estuaries and lagoons depend on the connection between freshwater and the sea. And for a rui in a Bengal pond and a bangda moving through the Arabian Sea, survival begins with the same question, asked in two very different ways: how do I keep the right amount of water inside my body? The answer is written into their gills, kidneys and cells — and eventually, into the way they reach our plates.
